newsitem.title: DUBAI: Gulf agencies fear proposed ban on tobacco ads.
newsitem.headline: Gulf agencies fear proposed ban on tobacco ads.

text.p: Advertising executives in the Gulf said on Sunday they were worried about a proposal by regional health ministers to ban media advertising of tobacco and related products, saying it could seriously damage the industry.

Late last month the ministers of health called on the Gulf Cooperation Council (GCC) general secretariat to consider the ban as part of its bid to crack down on smoking. The GCC is a political and economic forum comprising Saudi Arabia, the United Arab Emirates, Kuwait, Bahrain, Oman and Qatar.

Advertising executives said the proposed ban would strike a powerful blow to the region's young advertising sector and local economies. The Gulf is considered a major cigarette market, with imports in Saudi Arabia alone estimated to be worth about $800 million a year. Data for the whole Gulf were not available.

"The economic impact of tobacco advertising is big," Joseph Ghossoub, president of the International Advertising Association's UAE chapter, told Reuters. "The impact of stopping cigarette advertising is going to be felt by everybody."

The total spent on advertising for tobacco and related products by Gulf media stood at about $19 million in 1996, according to the Pan Arab Research Centre in Dubai. The figure leaps to about $28 million if "pan-Arab" media -- which cover other Arab countries in addition to Gulf states -- are included.
Ramzi Raad, executive vice president of advertising group Intermarkets, said the GCC plus pan-Arab advertising on tobacco had risen from $22.9 million in 1994 and $24.4 million in 1995.
Intermarkets' figures show tobacco advertising accounts for about five percent of GCC and pan-Arab media advertising expenditures of about $604 million in 1996.
"People in the industry are very concerned about this possible ban because it affects a key part of the advertising sector. It affects the industry overall," Ghossoub said.
Advertising executives said the ban would all but cripple some advertising agencies, who consider cigarette and tobacco product ads their bread and butter.

"It is not just going to affect the advertising agencies but the media too," one executive said. "The media will lose income from tobacco advertising, which is about 10 percent of the advertising income. They depend on advertising to survive."
Industry sources said they also feared the ban on media ads could just be the beginning of a series of new restrictions.

"We are very much afraid of the domino effect. Today you start by banning cigarette advertising and tomorrow you will get to chocolates and confectionery because you claim it will damage your children's teeth," one said.

He said he was afraid the ban might also be expanded to include cigarette advertising in general, including indirect advertising such as sponsorships. Tobacco firms are currently major sponsors of sporting and musical events in the Gulf.

The push to ban tobacco ads is a further step in GCC efforts to stamp out smoking. Gulf Arab states have started banning smoking on public transport and national airlines' domestic flights and routes between member states.
The alliance has also agreed to phase in increased customs duties on tobacco and related products to 100 percent by 2000.
Some Gulf states such as Oman have banned the import of cigarettes with more than 0.6 mg of nicotine and 10 mg of tar.
